source_text: Deus igitur machinator constitutorque rerum, sicut in se- s cundo libro diximus, antequam praeclarum hoc opus mundi adoriretur, sanctum et incorruptibilem spiritum genuit, quem filium nuncuparet. et quamuis alios postea innumerabiles creauisset, quos angelos dicimus, hunc tamen solum primogenitum diuini nominis appellatione dignatus est, patria scilicet uirtute ac maiestate pollentem. esse autem summi dei filium, qui sit potestate maxima praeditus, non tantum congruentes in unum uoces prophetarum, sed etiam Trismegisti praedicatio et Sibyllarum uaticinia demonstrant. Hermes in eo libro qui λόγος τέλειος inscribitur, his usus est uerbis: ὁ κύριος καὶ τῶν πάντων ποιητὴς, ὃν Θεὸν καλεῖν νενομίκαμεν, ἐπεὶ τὸν δεύτερον ἐποίησε θεὸν ὁρατὸν καὶ αἰσθητὸν — αἰσθητὸν δέ φημι οὐ διὰ τὸ αἰσθάνεσθαι αὐτὸν, περὶ γὰρ τούτου, πότερον αὐτὸς αἰσθάνεται ἣ μή, εἰσαῦθις ῥηθήσεται, ἀλλ᾽ ὅτι εἰς αἴσθησιν ὑποπέμπει καὶ εἰς ὅρασιν — ἐπεὶ οὖν τοῦτον ἐποίησε πρῶτον καὶ μόνον καὶ ἕνα, καλὸς δέ αὐτῷ ἐφάνη, καὶ πληρέστατος πάντων τῶν ἀγαθῶν, ἠγάσθη τε καὶ πάνυ ἐφίλησεν ὤς ἴδιον τόκον. Sibylla Erythraea in carminis sui Et rursus in fine eiusdem carminis: principio, quod a summo deo exorsa est, filium dei ducem et imperatorem omnium his uersibus praedicat: παντοτρόφον κτίστην, ὅστις γλυκὺ πνεῦμα ἅπασιν κάτθετο, χἠγητῆρα Θεὸν πάντων ἐποίησεν. et rursus in fine: ἄλλον ἔδωκε Θεὸς πιστοῖς ἀνδράσσι γεραίρειν. et alia Sibylla praecipit hunc oportere cognosci: αὐτὸν σου γίνωσκε Θεὸν Θεοῦ υἱὸν ἐόντα. uidelicet et ipse est dei filius, qui per Solomonem sapientissimum regem diuino spiritu plenum locutus est ea quae subiecimus: dominus condidit me initium uiarum suarum in opera sua, ante saeculum fundauit me: in principio antequam terram faceret et antequam abyssos constitueret, priusquam procederent fontes aquarum, ante omnes colles genuit me. dominus fecit regiones et fines inhabitabiles sub caelo. cum pararet caelum, aderam illi, etcum secerneret suam sedem: cum super uentos faceret ualidas nubes et cum confirmatos ponebat fontes sub caelo, quando fortia faciebat fundamenta terrae, eram penes illum disponens. ego eram cui adgaudebat. cottidie autem iucundabar ante faciem eius, cum laetaretur orbe perfecto. idcirco illum Trismegistus δημιουργὸν TOO seou et Sibylla σύμβουλον appellat, quod tanta sapientia et uirtute sit instructus a deo patre, ut consilio eius et manibus uteretur in fabricatione mundi.
pass_a_gloss: God therefore, the contriver and establisher of things, as we said in the second book, before this glorious work of the world was begun, generated a holy and incorruptible Spirit, whom He called Son. And although He afterwards created innumerable others, whom we call angels, He nevertheless deemed this one alone, the first-born, worthy of the divine name, clearly abounding in paternal virtue and majesty. That He is the Son of the highest God, endowed with the greatest power, is demonstrated not only by the congruent voices of the prophets, but also by the prediction of Trismegistus and the prophecies of the Sibyls. Hermes, in that book which is inscribed Logos Teleios, used these words: The Lord and maker of all things, whom we are accustomed to call God, since He made a second God visible and perceptible — I say perceptible, not because He is perceived, for it will be said again whether He perceives or not, but because He sends into perception and into sight — since, therefore, He made this one first and alone and single, and it seemed good to Him, and He was filled with all good things, He delighted in Him and loved Him exceedingly as His own offspring. The Erythraean Sibyl, in the beginning of her song, and again at the end of the same song, predicts the Son of God, the leader and commander of all, in these verses: the all-nourishing creator, who poured forth sweet spirit to all, and made God the leader of all. And again at the end: God gave another to faithful men to reverence. And another Sibyl commands that this one ought to be recognized: know Him as God, the Son of God being. Clearly, He is also the Son of God, who, through Solomon, the wisest king, full of the divine Spirit, spoke the things which we have subjoined: the Lord founded me in the beginning of His ways, in His works, before the century He founded me; in the beginning, before He made the earth, and before He established the abysses, before the fountains of waters proceeded, before all the hills He generated me. The Lord made the regions and the uninhabitable boundaries under the heaven. When He was preparing the heaven, I was with Him; when He was separating His seat, when He was making strong clouds over the winds, and when He was setting the confirmed fountains under the heaven, when He was making the strong foundations of the earth, I was with Him, arranging. I was the one in whom He delighted. Daily, however, I was rejoicing before His face, when He was rejoicing in the perfect orb. Therefore, Trismegistus calls Him the Demiurge, and the Sibyl calls Him the Counselor, because He is instructed by God the Father with such wisdom and virtue, that He uses His counsel and hands in the fabrication of the world.

pass_b_english: God, the architect and founder of all things — as we stated in the second book — brought forth a holy and incorruptible Spirit before beginning this glorious work of the world, and He named that Spirit His Son. Although He later created innumerable others whom we call angels, He honored this firstborn alone with the divine name, for He abounded in the Father's own virtue and majesty. That He is the Son of the Most High God, clothed with supreme power, is proved not only by the unanimous testimony of the prophets, but also by the prediction of Trismegistus and the oracles of the Sibyls. In the treatise entitled the Perfect Logos, Hermes writes: "The Lord and Maker of all things, whom we are accustomed to call God, since He made a second God, visible and perceptible — I say perceptible, not because He is perceived, for it will be stated again whether He Himself perceives or not, but because He conducts into perception and into sight — since therefore He made this one first, alone, and unique, and He appeared good to Him, and He was filled with all good things, He rejoiced in Him and loved Him exceedingly as His own offspring." The Erythraean Sibyl, at the opening of her poem and again at its close, proclaims the Son of God as leader and commander of all in these lines: "The all-nourishing Creator, who poured out sweet spirit upon all, and made God the leader of all." And again at the end: "God gave another to faithful men to reverence." Another Sibyl commands that this one must be recognized: "Know Him as God, for He is God's Son." Clearly He is also the Son of God who, through Solomon, the wisest king, filled with the divine Spirit, spoke the words we have appended: "The Lord possessed me at the beginning of His way, before His works of old. From everlasting I was established, from the beginning, before the earth existed. When there were no depths I was brought forth, when there were no springs abounding with water. Before the mountains were settled, before the hills, I was brought forth; while He had not yet made the earth or the fields, or the first of the dust of the world. When He established the heavens, I was there; when He drew a circle on the face of the deep, when He made firm the skies above, when He established the fountains of the deep, when He assigned the sea its limit so that the waters would not transgress His command, when He marked out the foundations of the earth, then I was beside Him, like a master workman; and I was daily His delight, rejoicing before Him always, rejoicing in His inhabited world and delighting in the children of man" (Proverbs 8:22-31). Therefore Trismegistus calls Him the Demiurge, and the Sibyl calls Him the Counselor, because God the Father has endowed Him with such wisdom and virtue that He employs His counsel and hands in fashioning the world.

review.notes: Pass B contains significant additions and fabrications not present in the Locked Latin. Specifically, in the Solomon/Proverbs section, Pass B adds: 'while He had not yet made the earth or the fields, or the first of the dust of the world', 'when He drew a circle on the face of the deep', 'when He assigned the sea its limit so that the waters would not transgress His command', 'like a master workman', and 'delighting in the children of man'. It also adds a scripture citation (Proverbs 8:22-31) which, while contextually appropriate for the allusion, is not in the source text. Pass B also translates 'ante saeculum' as 'From everlasting', whereas Pass A correctly renders it 'before the century' (or 'before the age').
